messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: IT Support
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 40

She was twenty-two years old, a radioman with a logistics unit in her home country’s army. The convoy was ambushed on a rural road at dusk. Mortars, then small arms fire. Her job was to call in support, but the radio went dead. She remembers the smell of diesel and wet earth, the sound of a man screaming in a language she could not quite place over the chaos. She pressed herself flat against the floor of the armored vehicle, counting her own breaths. When the shooting stopped, three soldiers from her company were dead. She was not physically hurt. For weeks afterward she told herself she was fine, that she had done her job, that the dead were just unlucky.

That was twenty-seven years ago. Now she is forty-nine, divorced, living alone in a one-bedroom apartment in a suburban city. She works IT support for a mid-size insurance company, taking calls from employees who cannot log in or whose printers have jammed. Her voice is calm and patient on the phone. She talks clients through rebooting their machines, step by step, never raising her voice. But when a call ends abruptly or a colleague pops into her cubicle without warning, her heart slams against her ribs. She needs a few seconds to steady her hands before she can type again.

She moved to the United States fifteen years ago, after marrying an American engineer she met online. The marriage lasted six years. She never told him the details of what happened in the convoy, only that she had served. He would ask why she flinched when he touched her shoulder from behind. She would say she was just jumpy. He grew frustrated. She grew quiet. The divorce was amicable on paper, but it left her with a deep sense of failure she cannot name.

At work, she keeps a small bottle of lavender oil in her desk drawer and dabs it on her wrists when the day feels too loud. She avoids the break room during lunch because the chatter and clatter of silverware remind her of the metal fragments rattling inside a medevac helicopter. She eats at her desk, alone. She has two close friends, both from a veterans’ support group she attended for a year. They text sometimes but rarely meet in person. She finds crowds exhausting. She stopped going to the grocery store on Saturdays.

She still has nightmares, though fewer than before. In the dream, she is back in the vehicle, and the radio crackles with static. She cannot make out the words. She wakes with her jaw clenched and a thin layer of sweat on her neck. On those mornings she takes a long shower, then drives to work fifteen minutes early to avoid traffic. She prefers the empty parking lot.

She has not spoken about the ambush in years. When a well-meaning coworker once asked about her military service, she said she did clerical work and changed the subject. She does not wear any insignia or veteran identifiers. On Independence Day, she stays inside with the windows closed and noise-canceling headphones on.

She is functional. Her clients rarely complain. Her supervisor appreciates her reliability. But she carries the ambush with her every day, not as a memory she tries to suppress, but as a low hum beneath everything else. She avoids loud noises, sudden movements, crowded hallways. She checks exits in restaurants automatically. She has not dated since the divorce. Some evenings she sits in her living room with the lights off, scrolling through her phone, waiting for the day to end.

She does not think of herself as a victim or a hero. She thinks of herself as someone who got through it and got on with life. But the getting on has required a kind of vigilance she rarely notices until a car backfires in the parking lot, and she finds herself under her desk, heart pounding, before she even knows she has moved.
